248.t: Bechet on the Smoky Mary, continued
248.s: Dawson repeats how he fetched sleeping Bechet from the train and sobered him up for the picnic; Bechet could really play.
248.q: Yeah, and they'd send me out there to go catch the train when it'd blow, it'd blow, you know. We'd be well over there in the camp. All the men, we done played a couple of numbers already waiting. I'd go out there and ask the conductor and fix him to go back and sit. I'd say, you seen a fellow…

248.t: Sidney Bechet asleep on the Smoky Mary
248.s: Dawson tells how he fetched a sleeping young Bechet from the train to Milneburg picnics, with Perez and Palao in the band.
248.q: We used to play at Millenburg for picnics out there. Those were only picnics. And Sidney Bechet, he was playing clarinet with us, you see. And well, and Manuel Perez was playing trumpet. And we had the same fella Jimmy Pollard playing violin too. He used to play with his two over there. And we'd…

248.t: The nickname 'Rat' and the Magnolia Band
248.s: Dawson explains how passing the hat got him called Rat, names the Magnolia Band players, and recalls Bechet and bands' habit of changing men.
248.q: Who were they? Yeah, Alphonse Peek Good and Javala. Where was it? That was down at Miller Phillips. I mean at Hunts and Nagels.

248.t: Freddie Keppard on violin and picnics with Manuel Perez
248.s: Keppard started on violin and took up a horn at picnics; Sidney Bechet's trouble with a train and wine is told.
248.q: He played that Dixieland and jazz trumpet just like the rest of them. Yeah. They all have to play that same way, you see, when you play the trumpet. Because when you get in a band, if you're playing trumpet in a band like they was playing then, you'd have to play that style, you know? The only…

619.t: Sidney Bechet's falling-out with his brother
619.s: Sidney and his brother Dr. Bechet became bitter, and Sidney stayed ragged with only his flute and clarinet.
619.q: Well, they got bitter against each other. That was so with him because he wouldn't do nothing but play that little flute and that clarinet after he got down to play a clarinet. And he stayed raggedy. He was raggedy as a jay boy.

619.t: Sidney Bechet as a boy and his return
619.s: Bechet grew up near Laurent, began on a cheap flute, played for a dollar a night, and later sold tunes for whiskey; Laurent met him at the airport.
619.q: Sidney brought up right by my house all these days. About the same age as you? He's just a few years older than me. He must have been around about four years older than me. But Sidney left here, when Sidney left here, and he didn't get back here in twenty some odd years. When Sidney got back here,…

619.t: Where Bechet lived and his first trip back in twenty years
619.s: He lists Bechet's addresses and says his brother only became proud of him after Laurent hosted him on that first return visit.
619.q: On Oakwood Street, yeah. He lived on Monroir Street. Then they moved to, his brother moved to St. Menard Street, but his brother got rid of him then. He moved to St. Menard and Moray. And from St. Menard and Moray he moved to St. Menard and Villaray.

76.t: Bechet at Nick's and getting Zutty out
76.s: Zutty got Bechet in at Nick's, where Nick disliked the fish horn, and Bechet later wanted the Spirits of Rhythm out and Zutty fired. Marge says he wanted to be the star and was mean.
76.q: I wish you would. Boy when I begged to Nick (Boyd Denicke) who (Bashey?) was, you know? So (Bashey?) played with us that night. He sat in with the band. And Nick told me he says, I don't like that fish horn. Get that fish horn out of here. Say I don't like it. So finally, (Bashey?) and the Spirits…

76.s: Bechet wrote to Zutty at the Alvin Hotel to join him in the Band Box with a long list of dos and don'ts; Marge tore it up. Dance adds that in the 1930s people called Bechet's vibrato corny.
76.q: He moved into the Alvin Hotel and he wanted you to be with his group. He was going to open across the street in the Band Box.

76.t: Bechet selfish; his villa and soprano-horn car in France
76.s: Zutty and Marge say Bechet could not be trusted and was selfish, yet in France he invited them and Lil Armstrong to his villa in Lille and drove them in a car whose horn played a saxophone riff.
76.q: But Zutty didn't know when we went to France. Oh he was so glad to see us. We were one of the few people that he had out to his villa you know. Because everybody, even the French ones, that's an honor because he has nobody out there. He doesn't invite anybody, he doesn't care who comes from…

35.t: Sidney Bechet as a reserved, hard-to-know man
35.s: Blumberg found Bechet quiet and difficult to talk to, though Wilbur took lessons from him.
35.q: Well, Bechet seems to be a very quiet guy, very difficult to get to know. He, he, uh, I think he kind of shut people out. I mean, that's the way, that's the impression I got anyway. Uh, because he's a very sensitive guy and, and often disturbed, I guess, with personal problems or, or who knows…

35.s: Russell recalls Bechet attending the Stuyvesant in January 1946 and Bunk playing his best toward him.
35.q: I was going to say, one night, uh, Sidney, uh, Boucher came in, uh, that was 19, uh, the, uh, January of 1946. It had been almost a year since they'd been in Boston together, but they hadn't forgotten any of it. And, but Sidney came up to the Stuyvesant to hear him one night and sat at the table.…

246.t: Dee Dee and Billy, Bucko Grammer, Albert Francis and young Bechet
246.s: Glass says Dee Dee and Billy started rehearsing at his house and lists men he played with, including Sidney Bechet as a boy.
246.ch: Bands, lake camps and early players
246.q: username. Who? Dee Dee. Well Dee Dee and Billy, well they know, you didn't know Dee Dee and Billy, but they started with me. Billy and Dee Dee was rehearsing at my house. That's where they started. Oh yeah? Billy and Dee Dee started right at my house. They practiced every day. It was Sunday. Billy…

246.t: Bechet and Paul Bond near his home; Raymond Glapion's photograph
246.s: Glass recalls Bechet on clarinet and Paul Bond on flute near his house, and promises to get a photograph of Raymond Glapion.
246.q: I thought he was dead. He is dead. I'm going to get his picture for you. His photograph.

23.t: Working with Bechet on soprano and his temperament
23.s: Rose says he gave Bechet a few soprano solos at concerts, and found him agreeable, simple and straightforward.
23.ch: Soprano sax and working with Bechet
23.q: Well, I was only, I always gave Bechet two or three solos to do in a concert on soprano sax. They were strictly solos with rhythm accompaniments. But at all other times he played the clarinet.

23.t: Bechet's musical judgment and suitable partners
23.s: Rose describes Bechet advising which trumpeters could play with him, rejecting Joe Thomas, and Max Kaminsky and Albert Nicholas working well with him.
23.ch: Soprano sax and working with Bechet
23.q: Oh, he certainly did. He had a very clear concept of what it was about. And he understood the role of his instrument. He also understood the role of the other instruments. And he was frequently frustrated by the fact that the other musicians frequently didn't understand. And I remember one time…

675.t: Bechet sits in with James Reese Europe's band
675.s: Braud tells how Europe and Noble Sissle heard Bechet and Bechet outplayed twelve clarinetists; he then contrasts bop with Dixieland and Ellington rhythm.
675.q: I was playing at the Mantis in 1917. James P. Europe from New York came then with his band, the 15th. That was one of the, at that time, they were one of the finest military bands I ever heard. And he had 12 clarinet players. So he came in the ducks and he listened to Sidney. So he called Sidney…

675.t: Sidney Bechet on soprano and clarinet
675.s: Braud praises Bechet's soprano and clarinet, his one-man-band record, and compares him to Bigard and Jimmy Noone.
675.q: No. Bache were playing clarinet at the time. And one of the best clarinet players ever left New Orleans or anybody's place. Because he, still today, I just heard him in Paris and I'm telling you, he's Mr. Paris. But he played the soprano. And right today, he played better clarinet than the average…

450.t: Paris elders and Mary Lou Williams sending her to hear Bechet
450.s: In Paris she met older musicians like Willie the Lion Smith and Bechet; Mary Lou Williams scolded her into hearing Sidney Bechet.
450.q: Well I’ve been blessed to have known them. I mean when I got to Paris there was Willie the Lion Smith, there was Bechet, there was Big Chief Russell Moore who played the tuba, there were a lot of people that were much older than I was, but we connected. And it’s called open up your ears and listen.…

450.t: Mary Lou Williams as a person and hearing Sidney Bechet
450.s: Ross remembers Williams as a funny, great cook who took her to hear Sidney Bechet, changing her mind about older jazz.
450.q: Yes, Pittsburgh. I always think of her with fondness and love.

1.t: Sidney Bechet's legend and Clarence Williams' recordings
1.s: Barker recalls players who left New Orleans before he could judge them, describes Bechet's reputation, and discusses Clarence Williams' business sense and borrowed tunes.
1.ch: Old New Orleans musicians and schooling
1.q: Red Allen. Guy Kelly. I didn’t see Jimmie Noone, because he left around 1917, 1918, ’19, ’20, and I wasn’t old enough to realize what I was looking at, knew who these people were. But I knew of them, that they went away. I heard of the Baquet family. I heard of Sidney Bechet. He was a legend. He…

1.t: Sidney Bechet in Europe and his soprano saxophone records
1.s: Barker explains that Bechet was abroad but his Wild Man Blues and one-man band records made him famous.

71.t: Playing the Brussels Fair with Sidney Bechet
71.s: Clayton recalls Bechet's fury over 'Royal Garden Blues' in Marseilles and then playing the 1958 Brussels Fair with him, Bechet's last engagement.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: But I had been there many times. I went and played at the World, Brussels Fair for Sidney Becket. Now this was in '58, 1958. This was Vic Dickenson, myself, Arvell Shaw, Kansas Fields, George Wein on the piano.

71.t: Bechet and the microphone; Teddy Buckner's high F
71.s: Bechet stayed in front of the microphone, overrode the trumpet, and got furious when Teddy Buckner hit a high F.
71.ch: Later tours, illness and the union job
71.q: Yes. I enjoyed it. I really enjoyed it. Especially Vic and myself. We hadn't been to Belgium before and seeing all of these buildings, this big Russian building where we'd gone in. They served you free vodka. So Vic stayed in there all day. And different shows from the East. And it was just great.

18.t: Sidney Bechet and the Saratoga Club records
18.s: He first met Bechet at the Saratoga Club and recalls a fine record with Sy Oliver arrangements.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: : We were, Uh, let's see. I was back, this was down in Saratoga, Club, and he came from Chicago, too, and (Errol Finan (?)) sat in with us and then I started making records with you know-

18.s: He loved Bechet and knows nothing of Creole versus other black musicians.
18.ch: Jazz opinions, Jelly Roll and the Rhythm Club
18.q: No, never. I don't know nothing about no Creole black musicians or nothing. I just know about people. 'Creole Lady' - name of the tune, that's about all I know. Chicago music and New Orleans music and all those kinds -

72.t: Giving Bechet a job at the Circle Ballroom
72.s: Bechet could not get a cabaret card, so Moore hired him in his band at a taxi-dance hall, where Bechet could not read stocks.
72.ch: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
72.q: Yeah. I met Bechet... I was working someplace... I think in the spare time I had... I was talking a few minutes ago about I had about a few weeks off or something...

72.t: Bechet in Brooklyn; rehearsals and Jimmy Ryan's
72.s: Moore rehearsed with Bechet at his Brooklyn apartment, with Bob Wilber on clarinet.
72.ch: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
72.q: I think he did. I'm not sure. Because he was... When I first met him, I think he was living...he was in Brooklyn. He was living in Brooklyn. We made recordings (I don't know if they ever came out or not) when he lived on Christie Street. That's when... He had an apartment on Christie Street. He was…

611.t: Sitting in with Sidney Bechet's band at the Vieux Colombier
611.s: Urged to visit Bechet in Paris, Waters borrowed Claude Luter's soprano, played so well the crowd roared, and Bechet through Jacques Butler banned him from the club out of jealousy.
611.ch: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
611.q: You know, I was - you ask these guys about anything, I could play the damn thing. I was playing real good soprano, see. Yes, he asked that guy who, very great soprano player around here, the guy that used to -

611.t: Visiting Bechet in Belgium, cleaning his pistol
611.s: Waters recalls going to Bechet's room at the casino in Belgium and finding him cleaning a pistol, and describes Bechet as a character and a big shot.
611.ch: Life in France and Sidney Bechet
611.q: Naah, nah. And then, and the last time I saw Sidney Bechet - well, not exactly the last time that I saw him in the theater but I was playing in a place called Cannuck [?], Belgium, which Cannuck, Belgium is considered the greatest - what do you call those things - casinos, supposed to be the…

388.t: Joining Sidney Bechet's quartet at Jimmy Ryan's
388.s: At Jimmy Ryan's across from the Three Deuces, Bechet takes Leeman with Kenny Kersey and Vic Dickenson; he was strict with drummers but seemed pleased.
388.q: On 52nd Street, I worked the other side of the coin, as they say. I went into the so-called Dixieland oriented club of Jimmy Ryan's across the street from the Three Deuces. I hadn't known Sidney previously, I believe Jimmy Ryan himself asked me or recommended me to Sidney, and Sidney asked if I'd…

388.t: The Bechet album recorded at the Rendezvous Club in Philadelphia
388.s: Leeman describes a French bootleg LP of the Bechet quartet with Kenny Kersey and Vic Dickenson, and how he adapted to Bechet's New Orleans style of snare and press rolls.
388.q: and I find it very hard, I'm trying to find out, I'm looking at the album now, it says 'recorded in the Rendezvous Club during his visit to the states" in '49 or '50. And he lived in France then and he visited here. The band was Vic Dickson, Kenny Kersey and myself, and the Rendezvous Club, it says…

30.t: Bechet covers his fingers from Paul Whiteman's saxophones
30.s: When Whiteman's saxophone section came to hear Bechet at Roseland, he draped a handkerchief over his mouthpiece and hands so they could not see his fingering.
30.q: And Bechet was funny because -- Paul Whiteman's group, they had heard about Bechet. So they were playing a dance at I think it was the Roseland and they all came over and Duke was playing, like, the intermission band, and all of Paul Whiteman's sax section came over there to hear. They wanted to…

30.t: Sidney Bechet could not read music
30.s: Bechet, as great as he was, could not read music; Bigard did not know him in New Orleans but met him later in New York.
30.q: Albert Nicholas and a couple of other guys. You see, as big as Sidney Bechet was, he couldn't read a note big as this whole house, and, like, he could play --

242.t: Sidney Desvigne, Earl Bostic and Desvigne's band
242.s: He recalls bands rehearsing in houses, hearing Desvigne's band with Earl Bostic as a boy, and later playing with Desvigne.
242.q: Sidney, yeah, when I, well, as you know, when I was a boy learning how to play music, at that time it was customary for the band to practice in houses at that time, see? And like, I mean, like today you say, well, I go to the union and they got a special place for bands to work. Well, it wasn't…

687.t: Working with Sidney Bechet and Tommy Ladnier in Noble Sissle's band
687.s: DeParis, Bechet and Ladnier were in Sissle's band for two years in Paris; Bechet and Ladnier played only solo and swing choruses, not section work.
687.q: Sidney and I worked together in in Noble Sissel's band oh for about two years or more we were in Paris together Sidney Tommy Ladner and myself and and then when he worked right here Jimmy Ryan's let me see I I worked with him one one stretch here and on record dates no around

768.t: Sidney Bechet joins the Deluxe band
768.s: Bechet joined the band after arriving with a show and quit when a pay mix-up showed Dewey earned more.
768.q: Yes. Well, after, after we were there, I don't know. I don't know exactly how long. But anyway, while we were at the Deluxe, Bichet came in town with a show. I think it was that Mary somebody's show. Mary Mack.

247.t: Old-time blues of 1904 and who played High Society
247.s: He insists the real old blues were played in 1904, and the talk turns to High Society and the clarinetist (Picou) who played it.
247.q: the name this song you just said? That's the blues. That's the blues. That's the real blues. Now the guy that St. Louis blues. You understand? That came later. Yeah, it comes later, yeah. But I'm talking about this old time blues I'm talking. And what year was that old time blues? That was in 1904.…

253.t: Sidney Bechet seen in New York and France
253.s: Hall speaks of soprano saxophonist Sidney Bechet, whom he met in New York after the war and visited in France.
253.q: After your buddy and a lot of those guys spoke about Sidney Bashier. Because they say he take a piano playing a drum and this is a soprano and go out on a clown and go out on a truck and give this band. He always, I always just like his playing. He always.

430.t: Sidney Bechet: the banana-coloured pawn-shop clarinet and a trumpet parade
430.s: Bechet is called the top clarinetist; Buddy Petit's band hired him and a pawn-shop clarinet was bought; he also once played trumpet in a parade.
430.q: Well, I remember at, at Villery and then they had a boy they called Williams, I can't think of his other name. He died in California. He and Basher tied up and it was, it was about even, even.

429.t: Sidney Bechet's playing and standing in France
429.s: Mike McKendrick was with Eddie South; Bechet led his own band, played clarinet and sax, and was beloved in France.
429.q: Eddie South's band. Eddie South was over there. You know who Sidney was playing with? No, with him. He played mostly with the white band, with the white fellas. Some of the French? Yeah, the French, yeah.

32.t: Sidney Bechet, William Marion Cook, Mary Wayne and Eugene Michael
32.s: The two discuss Bechet's trip with Cook, then White praises Cook, Mary Wayne's orchestra and his teacher Eugene Michael over Europe.
32.ch: Corrections and views on early Black music
32.q: And they might have introduced a sort of a modern aspect of a little ragtime with an interruption by him. But Sidney himself could not play qualifiedly in William Marion Cook's band at that time. No, he wasn't a good band.

2.t: The Esquire concert, Bechet and Louis, and a tape break
2.s: Dick Allen on the tradition's persistence, and Russell on the Esquire concert where Bechet and Louis clashed, ending with a tape change.
2.q: By the way, when they, they had an Esquire program, they had an all-star band, you know, Esquire. And so they gave some of the awards down here. I think it was a three-way hookup they had. Benny Goodman was in New York, somebody in San Francisco, and Louis, I believe, in New Orleans. The three of…

21.t: Jimmie Noone and Sidney Bechet as boys
21.s: He recalls Jimmie Noone and Sidney Bechet as young beginners.
21.q: Yeah. About Freddie. Freddie, uh, Jimmy Noon's sister was his lady friend, Freddie. Oh, yeah? And it was Joel Feene. That little Jimmy, I remember when he just started. Him and Sidney, basically.

892.t: Sidney Bechet as friend and a Bechet record
892.s: Mary calls Bechet a great friend of Lee and mentions a photograph; the host plays Bechet's KC Man Blues.
892.q: Right. I'm sorry. Uh-huh. Sidney Bichet, well, he was our great friend. Also, I have, I will show you, I have a photograph of Lee and Sidney.

734.t: Baquet, Bechet, Johnny Dodds and reading at the Villa
734.s: Baquet played straight; Bechet clean in style; Dodds tied keys down; reading music at the Villa.
734.q: Well, he played equally wonderful, and I liked his style, you know, that's what I say. He played some kind of, but he used to cut in, you know, so much, that funny stuff, but he was clean, you know, with it, you know. A fella can be clean with his style, you know.

590.t: Sidney Bechet's friendship with Armstrong and staying in Paris
590.s: Bechet and Armstrong stayed friends, and Bechet remained in Europe where he was like a king.
590.q: Yeah. They did, you know? Uh-huh. Sometimes you guys have a little thing they don't like. Sometimes they... I'm sorry. They died friends. I mean you made like a little arguments or something. Oh well no. But I mean they're all friends.

48.t: Sidney Bechet and his brother Leonard; Big Eye Louis
48.s: Playing with Bechet before he left New Orleans, his sitting in, and Dr. Leonard Bechet.
48.q: Did you ever play with Sidney? Yeah, sure. Sidney come up right around me. He did. We played together several times. Sidney Bichet. He's nice too.

591.s: They became close friends; Goudie visited Bechet in Paris after the war and discusses recordings with Noble Sissle.
591.q: Well, I was there when it happened and he had to leave and I had to bring that up, but it's the truth anyway. The truth can be put on that. It's living. And when he came back, he, ten years after that, he came back and he, when he went, when he got out and I wanted to help him. He said, if you need…

1006.t: Johnny Dodds and Sidney Bechet as boys
1006.s: Johnny Dodds started on a tin flute before clarinet, as did Bechet; Alexis took a girl from Sidney in their knee-pants days.
1006.q: I took a girl from Sidney back on Marilyn Johnson when we was in the knee pants. You're an expert at taking girls. When we were in the knee pants, Marilyn Johnson. Our name was B.B. Nice little little Creole guy.

53.t: George Baquet and young Sidney Bechet
53.s: Billy and Allen try to recall George Baquet of Philadelphia, and Billy remembers Sidney Bechet as a boy playing a clarinet held together with wire.
53.q: You didn't? No. Oh, he had a whole way in quite a few of those. What's this fellow's name in Philadelphia from the Orleans? George something. George Bishop, not Bishop.

858.t: Idols Paul Barnes and Bonnie Begarde
858.s: Johnson names Paul Barnes and Bonnie Begarde as his favorite musicians and what instruments each played.
858.q: Yeah. He was a saxophone player, and saxophone player, yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah, that was it. Paul Barnes and Bonnie Begarde is my two favorite musicians.

198.t: Sidney Bechet and young Barnes cutting heads around age 17
198.s: Barnes recalls Bechet as a younger boy he played with, and how they went around town challenging other clarinetists; he describes his 13-key Buffet.
198.q: you know yeah he'd do all kinds of variations yeah he was on the auto of bishay see that's the way i got it just on the bishay what bishay after later on bishay had stopped a whole lot of work but bishay's a pretty kind man he would take on the better off the second piece up and he said play do a…

521.s: Asked about early artists, she shows a Bechet photo by Frank Wolff; she did not follow pressing numbers or the business side.
521.q: Well among the first who became very popular, I think we have a picture maybe we can show of Sidney Bechet. You knew – he had a great career in France, and of course he came here and he was recognized too. But maybe we’ll show these later. But here we have him looking — Frank took this picture in…

448.t: Bechet as artist, European tour and self-taught youth
448.s: Bechet's rhythm teaching, his 1919 trip with Cook's orchestra, ambitions for serious music, and self-taught early life.
448.q: Yeah. And he’d explain about jazz rhythm, he says jazz rhythm, you’ve got that steady beat going here, and then you introduce rhythms against the steady beat. That’s what jazz is. [scats] That’s what you’ve got to do, that steady beat and then those rhythms against it. He had a very strong idea…

370.t: Sidney Bechet and the small Blue Note office
370.s: Gordon describes Bechet's visits and cooking, the Summertime hit, Mezz Mezzrow's family, Alfred's mother Margarita, and her own office chores.
370.ch: Sidney Bechet and the Blue Note office
370.q: You know, it’s just a normal young girl, growing up, meeting interesting people. That was my... Music brought me in to those people. Lucky me. Well, that’s just the way your life goes. You never know which way it’s going to turn. I loved Sidney Bechet. I was just reading in a book he was in Europe,…

123.t: Bechet records and his early heroes
123.s: He names his first 78 as a Sidney Bechet record, says he never heard Bechet live, and names Red Allen and J.C. Higginbotham as heroes.
123.q: No I never did. I heard Bob Wilbur who was his disciple. He was pretty good, but... in fact I think he’s still going.

406.t: Sidney Bechet as an early influence; later study with Joe Allard
406.s: He listened to Bechet alongside Hawkins and learned 'Wildcat Blues' in 1923. In New York he studied some clarinet with Joe Allard.
406.ch: Fletcher Henderson, Ella Fitzgerald and the early 1940s
406.q: Well, at the same time that I was listening to Coleman Hawkins I was listening to Bechet, when he was playing the clarinet and soprano saxophone. And, in fact, in 1923 I learned a solo that he played called 'Wildcat Blues.' I still play it today. I have an arrangement on it and I feature it on the…

26.t: Bechet's character and the Salem Willows cab ride
26.s: Greer calls Bechet beautiful and tells of a summer job for Charlie Shribman and a costly night cab ride.
26.ch: The Washingtonians, Bechet and drum style

87.s: Willard cites Duke's four favorites; Young calls Bechet daring and reckless, jammed with him in Paris, and notes the statue in France.

106.t: Bechet's clarinet playing and the blues
106.s: Bechet played clarinet in 1919, not yet soprano, and was a blues specialist; the orchestra's program listed his 'Characteristic Blues' alongside one-steps and fox-trots.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: Not the soprano, because the soprano is another story. He started the soprano. I was with him when he got his first soprano in London.

146.ch: Opening and early years in Dallas
146.q: Yes. But he was playing the soprano sax, and I tried to copy behind him. I'd buy all his records and listen to him. Sidney Bechet.

379.s: Bechet played only solos and was later forgotten.
379.q: Well, now, since you mentioned that -- I'm glad you mentioned that, because he had a distinctive way of playing. Nobody played like -- to me, the way we played. And they used him in the band just for solo. He didn't play no parts with the rest of the saxophones.

28.s: In France the second time, Bechet showed off his new Lincoln, which hid a rifle over the windshield, a carbine, a .45 under the dash and more.

Said, if anybody bothers me, I'm going to show you what I'll do, and he pulled out a rifle. See, he reached up, he had a place built in that -- over the windshield, and pulled out…

69.s: He heard Bechet in New York and admired his New Orleans style.
69.q: Well, what he was playing was terrific, you know? He was that real New Orleans style, you know, that Dixieland and so forth.

92.t: Sidney Bechet and Benny Carter as giants
92.s: He heard Bechet with Noble Sissle's band, with Eddie Cole on bass, and praises Benny Carter's cultured style.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: No, I just -- I wanted to mention Sidney Bechet who was one of the great saxophonists, you know, and a lot of the musicians aren't aware of how great he was. He was with Noble Sissle's band, and I used to go to see them

94.t: Bechet's 'Who's that boy?' story with Red Richards
94.s: On the way to Toronto Bechet repeatedly failed to recognize Red Richards.
94.ch: Sidney Bechet and the Paris festival
94.q: It was nice to be with Bechet because he taught me all about traditional jazz and now, and "Shimmy-Shewabble," ...them tunes. what to do with the "Muskrat Ramble" /"My Maryland," I liked the way he did "My Maryland." 412.t: The Sidney Bechet no-show and the union hearing
412.s: Bechet failed to turn up for the first week, then showed and demanded pay. Hodes refused, and Bechet took him to the union. Hodes then paid him, and Bechet became a friend on later Blue Note dates.
412.ch: Radio, Jazz Record and Blue Note (Reel 2)
412.q: Trombone, Sandy Williams, -- I don't know who else was around. But these were the musicians that -- Sidney Bechet, I had Sidney many times. In fact, I've got a story about Sidney. This was the first time I had Sidney. I hired him, I told him the date. Everybody showed up but Sidney. Well, I'm in a…

95.s: She loved Bechet's sax, always asked for him on records, and says her brother kept men from speaking to her.
95.q: I loved that sax he played, I loved that sax that Bichet played. Everytime I'd go to record, they'd say, 'Who do you want ?' I'd say, 'Bichet.'

112.t: Head arrangements and Sidney Bechet's Dear Old Southland
112.s: After Bricktop introduces Sidney Bechet, he plays Dear Old Southland on soprano and makes Wooding's arrangement obsolete.
112.q: Yeah, well like a head. And we'd put an introduction on it, maybe a four bar introduction, and then we'd put maybe a couple of bars to make a first ending or a second ending.
